If the doji gapped away from that body instead, it would be in star position, as in a doji star. Engulfing is the reverse, with a big second body covering the first.
questions.lesson_line: A doji inside a long body is a harami cross. A doji that gaps away is a doji star.

wrong.Morning doji star: In a doji star the doji gaps away from the first candle. Here it sits inside the first body.
wrong.Bullish engulfing: Engulfing needs a big second body covering the first. A doji has almost no body.
wrong.Spinning top: A spinning top is one candle with a small real body and long shadows. This is two candles, and the second is a doji.

questions.simple: It is a harami cross, because the second candle is a doji that sits inside the first candle's body.

questions.story: A stock has rallied for two weeks. Day 1 is a long white candle from $40.00 to $44.00. Day 2 opens at $43.20 and closes at $42.80.
questions.q: The two days make which pattern?
questions.why: Bearish harami. Day 2's small body, $43.20 to $42.80, sits inside Day 1's long white body from $40.00 to $44.00. It came after a two-week advance, so it is the bearish kind. After a decline, a harami is read as a potential bullish reversal.
questions.lesson_line: Body inside body makes a harami. The trend before it says which kind.

wrong.Bearish engulfing: Engulfing needs the second body to swallow the first. Day 2's body is the smaller one.
wrong.Dark cloud cover: A dark cloud opens above Day 1's close. Day 2 opened at $43.20, below Day 1's $44.00 close.
wrong.Evening star: An evening star takes three candles, and its small middle one gaps above the first body. Day 2 opened at $43.20, inside Day 1's body, and no third day is given.

questions.simple: It's a bearish harami, because Day 2's small body sits inside Day 1's long white body after a rally.

questions.q: A bearish harami after a rally means the stock will turn down.
questions.why: False. ChartSchool calls a harami after an advance a potential bearish reversal, not a sure one. Most bearish patterns need confirmation. Fidelity's slides add that many report the harami can break either way. ChartSchool says the small second candle shows consolidation, so read it as a pause. Do not act until a breakout in one direction activates it.
questions.lesson_line: A harami is a pause. The break that follows tells you which way.
questions.simple: False, because a bearish harami only hints at a turn, and it needs the next candles to confirm it.

deeper.trap: The name sounds like a forecast. Bearish harami tells you where it formed, after an advance, not what comes next. Fidelity's slides say that although common belief is that the harami is a reversal pattern, many report it can break either way. Treat it as a pause and let the break pick the side.

questions.q: What is an inside day?
choices: High and low inside the prior range
Body inside the prior day's body
Smaller range than the prior day
Open and close about the same price
questions.answer: High and low inside the prior range
questions.why: High and low inside the prior range. The whole day, shadows included, fits within the day before. Investopedia says it shows reduced volatility and consolidation. It is not a harami, which only needs the body inside the prior body.
questions.lesson_line: Inside day is range inside range. It shows the stock tightening up.

wrong.Body inside the prior day's body: That's a harami. An inside day looks at the high and low, not just the body.
wrong.Smaller range than the prior day: A smaller range alone isn't enough. The high and low must both sit within the prior day's range.

questions.simple: It is an inside day when its high and low both stay within the prior day's range, which shows the stock tightening.

questions.story: Monday: open $49.00, high $52.00, low $48.00, close $49.40. Tuesday: open $50.50, high $51.20, low $48.90, close $50.80.
questions.q: Tuesday is best called what?
questions.why: Inside day. Tuesday's range, $48.90 to $51.20, sits completely within Monday's $48.00 to $52.00 range. It is not a harami: Tuesday's body, $50.50 to $50.80, sits above Monday's $49.00 to $49.40 body, not inside it. An inside day tests the range, and a harami tests the body. It shows lower volatility, but it does not tell you which way the breakout will go.
questions.lesson_line: Check the range for an inside day and the body for a harami. They're different tests.

wrong.Harami: A harami's body sits inside the prior body. Tuesday's body, $50.50 to $50.80, is above Monday's $49.00 to $49.40 body.
wrong.Outside day: An outside day breaks both the prior high and the prior low. Tuesday did neither.
wrong.Bullish engulfing: Engulfing needs Tuesday's body to cover Monday's. The two bodies don't even overlap.

questions.simple: Tuesday is an inside day, because its high and low stay within Monday's range, while its body sits above Monday's body.

deeper.trap: The two tests can split. A day can sit inside the prior range while its body sits outside the prior body, as here. It can also go the other way: a small body inside the prior body, with a high above the prior high. That is a harami but not an inside day, since a harami's shadows need not fit inside.

questions.q: An inside day usually points to the direction of the next breakout.
questions.why: False. An inside day shows the range narrowing and volatility easing. Investopedia says the breakout direction can't be predicted from the pattern alone. Fidelity's inside-bar plan has an entry both ways. It buys on an open above the inside bar close and sells on an open below it. The day's high and low give you the levels to watch.
questions.lesson_line: An inside day gives you levels, not direction. Its high and low are the lines to watch.
questions.simple: False, because an inside day only shows the range getting smaller, not which way the stock will break.

deeper.trap: A tight day can feel like a hint about direction. It is not a forecast. Investopedia says a series of inside days may signal a coming reversal. Yet the breakout direction can't be predicted from the pattern alone. Plan for both sides and let price choose.

questions.q: What is an outside day?
choices: Higher high and lower low than prior
High and low both inside the prior range
Body swallows the prior day's body
Gaps above the prior day's high
questions.answer: Higher high and lower low than prior
questions.why: Higher high and lower low than the prior day. Its range covers the whole prior day, shadows included. It is not the same as engulfing. Engulfing only needs the second body to cover the first body. An outside day needs the whole range covered, at both ends.
questions.lesson_line: Outside day: range covers range, at both ends.

wrong.Body swallows the prior day's body: That's engulfing, which only needs the bodies. An outside day needs the whole range.
wrong.Gaps above the prior day's high: A gap up only says where it opened. An outside day must trade both above the prior high and below the prior low.
wrong.High and low both inside the prior range: That's an inside day, the opposite.

questions.simple: An outside day trades above the prior day's high and below its low, so its range covers the whole day before.

questions.story: A stock has rallied for three weeks. Today it trades above yesterday's high, then falls below yesterday's low. It closes down near the low.
questions.q: Today is best described as what?
questions.why: Outside reversal day. It is an outside day, with a high above yesterday's high and a low below yesterday's low. It also closes in the opposite direction of the prior trend. After a rally, that means a down close. Investopedia notes analysts pair it with volume or support levels for more reliability. It signals a potential trend change, not a certain one.
questions.lesson_line: An outside day that closes against the trend is an outside reversal. Volume and the level it hits add weight.

wrong.Inside day pattern: An inside day stays within yesterday's range. Today broke out of both ends.
wrong.Harami cross: A harami cross needs a doji tucked inside the prior body. Today's range swallowed yesterday's.
wrong.Morning star: A morning star is a three-candle turn after a decline. This is one day, after a rally.

questions.simple: It is an outside reversal day, because it broke both ends of yesterday's range and closed down against the rally.

deeper.trap: Don't mix it up with bearish engulfing. Engulfing only needs today's body to cover yesterday's body. ChartSchool says the outside reversal needs the entire range engulfed, high and low, not just the open and close. So a day can be one without being the other. Check the shadows, then the close against the trend.

questions.q: When does a candle sit in star position?
choices: Its small body gaps from the prior body
It opens at the prior candle's close
It has no shadow above or below its body
It closes right at the session's high
questions.answer: Its small body gaps from the prior body
questions.why: When its small body gaps away from the prior candle. A candle that gaps away from the one before it is in star position. It looks isolated from the price action before it. The gap can be up or down. The star itself has a small body: doji, hammers, shooting stars and spinning tops can all sit there. It is not about shadows or where the candle closes.
questions.lesson_line: A star is a small body standing apart after a gap. It's the middle of the morning and evening star.

wrong.It opens at the prior candle's close: Then there is no gap. A star gaps away from the candle before it.
wrong.It has no shadow above or below its body: That describes a marubozu. A star is about the gap, not the shadows.
wrong.It closes right at the session's high: Where it closes in its own range doesn't make a star. The gap does.

questions.simple: A candle is in star position when its small body gaps away from the candle before it and stands apart.

questions.q: A long black candle, a small candle that gaps down, then a long white candle closing past the black's midpoint. Which word?
questions.why: Morning star. It takes three candles, and it should form within a downtrend. First a long black candle. Then a small candle that gaps below the black close. Then a long white candle that closes above the midpoint of the first body. The third candle is the confirmation. If the middle candle is a doji, it is a morning doji star.
questions.lesson_line: Morning star: down, pause, up. The third candle is the one that does the work.

wrong.Evening star: That's the bearish mirror, which forms after an advance. Here the first candle is black.
wrong.Three white soldiers: That's three long white candles in a row. The first candle here is black.
wrong.Bullish harami: A harami is two candles, with the second inside the first. This takes three, and the middle one gaps away.

questions.simple: It is a morning star: a long black candle, a small candle that gaps lower, then a long white candle.

questions.q: What is an evening star?
choices: Up candle, small gap-up, down candle
Down candle, small gap-down, up candle
Three long down candles in a row
Up candle, then a doji inside it
questions.answer: Up candle, small gap-up, down candle
questions.why: Up candle, small gap-up, down candle. First a large white candle. Then a small candle that gaps above the first body, showing the advance has stalled. Then a down candle completes it. It is the mirror of the morning star, which forms in a downtrend. Three black candles in a row would be three black crows instead.
questions.lesson_line: Evening star: up, pause, down. The small middle candle is the pause.

wrong.Down candle, small gap-down, up candle: That's the morning star, the mirror image after a decline.
wrong.Up candle, then a doji inside it: That's a harami cross. A star's middle candle gaps away from the first.

questions.simple: An evening star is a large up candle, then a small candle that gaps above it, then a down candle.

questions.q: In a morning star, the small middle candle can be either white or black.
questions.why: True. ChartSchool describes the middle candle as a small white or black candle that gaps below the prior close. Investopedia agrees it can be black or white. What makes it a star is the small body and the gap down. If it is a doji, the pattern is called a morning doji star.
questions.lesson_line: In a star pattern, the middle candle's size and gap matter. Its color doesn't.
questions.simple: True, because the middle candle's small body and its gap matter, not its color.

questions.story: Day 1 is a long black candle from $50.00 down to $45.00. Day 2 gaps lower and opens and closes at $44.20. Day 3 opens at $45.20 and closes at $48.50.
questions.q: Name the three-day pattern.
questions.why: Morning doji star. Day 1 is a long black candle from $50.00 down to $45.00. Day 2 gaps lower and opens and closes at $44.20, a doji below the black close. Day 3 is a long white candle that closes at $48.50, above the middle of Day 1's body. It is a morning star whose middle candle is a doji.
questions.lesson_line: When the small middle candle is a doji, the morning star becomes a morning doji star.

wrong.Evening doji star: That's the top version: long white, doji, long black.
wrong.Harami cross: In a harami cross the doji sits inside the first body. Here the doji gapped below it.
wrong.Three white soldiers: That needs three long white candles. Day 1 is black and Day 2 is a doji.

questions.simple: It is a morning doji star, because a doji gaps below a long black candle before a long white candle.

deeper.trap: Check where the doji sits. Below the first body, after a gap, it is in star position, so this is a morning doji star. Inside the first body, the same doji would make a harami cross. The doji looks the same in both. Its position names the pattern.

questions.q: What are three white soldiers?
choices: Three long white candles in a row
Three small candles in a big one
Three long black ones in a row
questions.answer: Three long white candles in a row
questions.why: Three long white candles in a row. Each one opens within the prior candle's real body. ChartSchool adds that each close should be near the day's high, and Investopedia that it tops the prior candle's high. So the soldiers do not gap up at the open. The mirror pattern, three long black candles, is three black crows.
questions.lesson_line: Soldiers march up, crows fly down. Both are three long bodies in a row.

wrong.Three small candles in a big one: That's the middle of a rising three methods.
wrong.Three white candles gapping up: Each soldier opens inside the prior candle's body, not above it. A gap up at each open breaks that rule.

questions.simple: Three white soldiers are three long white candles in a row, each opening inside the body before it.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Three long black candles in a row, each closing near its low, are called ___.
questions.why: Three black crows. ChartSchool describes three long black bodies in a row. Each opens within the prior body and closes at or near its low. Schwab adds that they close progressively lower. Three white soldiers is the up version. As a bearish reversal pattern, it needs an uptrend before it.
questions.lesson_line: Three black crows show sellers in charge three sessions running.
questions.simple: Three black crows, because three long black candles in a row, each closing near its low, show sellers in charge.

questions.q: A long white candle, three small candles inside its range, then a white candle closing at a new high. Which word?
questions.why: Rising three methods. A long white candle comes first. Then three small candles stay within its high and low. Then a fifth candle closes at a new high. ChartSchool calls it a bullish continuation pattern, so it shows a rest inside an advance, not a turn.
questions.lesson_line: Rising three methods is a rest inside a big up candle, then a push to a new high.

wrong.Three white soldiers: That's three long white candles back to back, with no small ones resting between.
wrong.Bullish harami: A harami is two candles. This pattern takes five.
wrong.Morning star: A morning star starts with a long black candle after a decline. This starts with a long white one.

questions.simple: It is rising three methods, because small candles rest inside a long white candle's range before a push to a new high.

questions.q: You should act on a candle pattern only after a breakout activates it.
questions.why: True. Fidelity warns not to act on a perceived candle pattern until a breakout in one direction activates it. ChartSchool agrees that most reversal patterns require confirmation. For a bullish pattern that means more upside follow-through. That can be a gap up, a long white candle or a high volume advance.
questions.lesson_line: A candle pattern asks a question. The next candle answers it.
questions.simple: True, because a pattern is just a first hint until a breakout in one direction backs it up.

reasons: fixed before (checker corrected the Schwab sentence)

questions.story: After a two-week slide, a stock prints a bullish engulfing. The next day it gaps down and closes below the engulfing candle's low.
questions.q: What's your read on the pattern now?
choices: Confirmed: a gap down is a dip to buy
Unconfirmed, but buy: the shape is good
questions.why: Unconfirmed. Bullish confirmation means more upside after the pattern, such as a gap up, a long white candle or a high volume advance. Investopedia names a move above the engulfing candle's high as the confirmation. This stock did the opposite. It gapped down and closed below the engulfing candle's low. A textbook shape counts for little once the next day disagrees.
questions.lesson_line: The pattern asked a question and the next day said no. I'd rather wait than argue with it.

wrong.Confirmed: the shape was textbook: Shape alone never confirms. ChartSchool wants further strength after the pattern.
wrong.Confirmed: a gap down is a dip to buy: A gap down is the opposite of follow-through. ChartSchool wants further strength after the pattern, and this close sits below its low.
wrong.Unconfirmed, but buy: the shape is good: Fidelity warns not to act on a candle pattern until a breakout activates it. Here the break went down, not up.

questions.simple: It is unconfirmed, because the next day gapped down and closed below the pattern's low instead of following through higher.

deeper.trap: A perfect shape tempts you to buy anyway. But the shape only asks a question. ChartSchool wants further strength to confirm a bullish reversal. Investopedia names a move above the engulfing candle's high as the trigger. A close below its low is the opposite answer.

questions.q: A bullish engulfing pattern that prints at a new high is still a bullish reversal pattern.
questions.why: False. A bullish reversal pattern should form within a downtrend. ChartSchool says a bullish engulfing at new highs can hardly be considered a bullish reversal pattern. It shows continued buying pressure and could count as a continuation pattern. Fidelity's slides say candle patterns are traditionally used to spot a trend that is ending. At a new high there is no downtrend to end.
questions.lesson_line: Check the trend before you name the pattern. No downtrend, no bullish reversal.
questions.simple: False, because a reversal needs a trend to reverse, and at a new high there is no downtrend to turn.

deeper.counter: Same shape, two meanings. After a two-week slide, a bullish engulfing is a possible reversal that still needs confirmation. At a new high, ChartSchool reads it as continued buying, closer to a continuation pattern. Name the trend first, then the pattern.

reasons: key rests on one publisher (ChartSchool f71, f16, f70); Investopedia f136 supports only the bearish mirror

questions.story: Yesterday a stock closed at $50.00. Today it gaps up, opens at $53.00, drifts lower and closes at $52.00.
questions.q: Is today's candle hollow or filled?
choices: Filled: it closed below its open
Neither: it's a doji, a thin line
Hollow: buyers gapped it up at the open
questions.answer: Filled: it closed below its open
questions.why: Filled. The fill compares today's $52.00 close with today's $53.00 open, not with yesterday's $50.00 close. A close below the open draws a filled candle, with the open at the top of the body. It is filled even though the stock is up on the day.
questions.lesson_line: A filled candle can still be up on the day. The fill compares the close with its own open.

wrong.Hollow: it's up from yesterday: The day's change doesn't decide the fill. A close below the open makes it filled.
wrong.Neither: it's a doji, a thin line: A doji needs the open and close about equal. $53.00 down to $52.00 is a real body.
wrong.Hollow: buyers gapped it up at the open: The gap sets where it opened, not the fill. The $52.00 close below the $53.00 open makes it filled.

questions.simple: It's filled, because the $52.00 close is below the $53.00 open, even though the stock is up on the day.

questions.q: A candlestick and a regular price bar show the same four prices.
questions.why: True. Both show the open, high, low and close for each period. A bar marks them with simple lines, and a candle draws the open-to-close part as a colored body. The data is the same. A line chart is different: it connects only the closing prices.
questions.lesson_line: Bars and candles hold the same data. Candles make the open-close story easier to see.
questions.simple: True, because a candle and a price bar both show the open, high, low and close, just drawn in different ways.

questions.story: A stock opens at $30.00 and sells off to $27.50 by midday. By the close it is back at $30.40, near the high.
questions.q: What does the long lower shadow tell you?
choices: Buyers took back a deep drop
Heavy volume came in at the low
questions.answer: Buyers took back a deep drop
questions.why: Buyers took back a deep drop. Sellers drove it down to $27.50 during the session. Buyers then bid it back up to close at $30.40, above the $30.00 open. ChartSchool reads a long lower shadow this way: sellers dominated, then buyers resurfaced for a strong close. It describes today only. It does not promise a higher close tomorrow.
questions.lesson_line: A long lower shadow shows where buyers showed up. It describes today; it doesn't promise tomorrow.

wrong.Sellers controlled the close: The close was near the high. CME reads a small body near the top as buyers taking control by the end.
wrong.It will go higher tomorrow: A candle describes one session. Fidelity warns not to act on a pattern until a breakout activates it.
wrong.Heavy volume came in at the low: A candle holds only the open, high, low and close. It does not show volume. Check the volume bars for that.

questions.simple: Buyers took back a deep drop, because sellers pushed it to $27.50 but buyers lifted it to close above the open.

questions.story: A stock at new highs spikes 6% in the first hour. By the close it has given almost all of it back and finishes near its open.
questions.q: What does the long upper shadow tell you?
choices: Buyers won: it made a new high
Sellers will push it lower tomorrow
questions.why: Sellers pushed back the rally. Buyers bid it up early and set a new high. By the close, sellers had forced it back near the open. ChartSchool reads a long upper shadow as buyers dominating during the session, then sellers forcing prices down from their highs. It shows the rally failed today. It does not say what happens next.
questions.lesson_line: A long upper shadow is a rally that didn't hold. The close tells you who won the day.

wrong.Buyers held the day's gains: They didn't. It finished near the open after spiking 6%.
wrong.Buyers won: it made a new high: It touched a new high but couldn't hold it. The close near the open says sellers won the back half.
wrong.Sellers will push it lower tomorrow: One candle describes one session. ChartSchool says most bearish patterns require bearish confirmation, so wait for the next candle.

questions.simple: Sellers pushed back the rally, because the stock spiked early but closed near its open after giving almost all of it back.

deeper.trap: At a new high, a long upper shadow feels like the top. It might not be. Schwab says signs that a rally may be ending usually amount to yellow flags, not red ones. ChartSchool says most bearish patterns require bearish confirmation. Note the high it rejected and watch what the next candle does.

questions.q: Open $40.00, high $41.50, low $39.60, close $41.20. How big is the real body?
questions.why: $1.20. The real body is the range between the open and the close: $41.20 minus $40.00. The high of $41.50 and the low of $39.60 make the shadows, and they are left out. The close is above the open, so this body is hollow.
questions.lesson_line: Body is close minus open. Leave the high and the low out of it.
questions.simple: The real body is $1.20, because it runs from the $40.00 open to the $41.20 close, and the shadows don't count.

wrong.$1.90: Used high minus low, which counts the shadows.
wrong.$1.50: Measured open to the high, which counts the upper shadow.
wrong.$1.60: Measured low to the close, which adds the lower shadow.

questions.q: Open $25.00, high $27.40, low $24.80, close $25.30. How long is the upper shadow?
questions.why: $2.10. The close, $25.30, is above the open, $25.00, so the close is the top of the body. The upper shadow runs from there to the $27.40 high: $27.40 minus $25.30. Do not measure from the open, which is the bottom of this body.
questions.lesson_line: Upper shadow is the high minus the top of the body. On a hollow candle, the top is the close.
questions.simple: The upper shadow is $2.10, because it runs from the $25.30 close at the body's top to the $27.40 high.

wrong.$2.40: Measured from the open, which is the bottom of this body.
wrong.$2.60: Used high minus low, the whole range.
wrong.$2.30: Added the lower shadow, which is not part of the upper one.

questions.q: Open $60.00, high $60.10, low $57.00, close $59.40. How long is the lower shadow?
questions.why: $2.40. The close, $59.40, is below the open, $60.00, so the candle is filled and the close is the bottom of the body. The lower shadow runs from $59.40 down to the $57.00 low. Measuring from the open would count the body as part of the shadow.
questions.lesson_line: On a filled candle the bottom of the body is the close. Measure the lower shadow from there.
questions.simple: The lower shadow is $2.40, because on this filled candle the bottom of the body is the $59.40 close.

deeper.trap: One easy slip is to measure every lower shadow from the open. That works only on a hollow candle, where the open is the bottom of the body. On a filled candle the close is the bottom, so start there. From the $60.00 open you would be adding the whole body to the shadow.

wrong.$0.60: That is the body, not the lower shadow.
wrong.$0.70: Measured up from the close to the high, which is not the lower shadow.
wrong.$0.10: That is the upper shadow: the high minus the open.

questions.story: A stock has slid for a month. Today it opens at $22.00, rallies to $24.10, and fades to close at $22.50. The low is $21.90.
questions.q: Which word fits today's candle?
questions.why: Inverted hammer. The body is small and near the low, from $22.00 to $22.50. The upper shadow runs up to $24.10, and the lower shadow is tiny. It came after a month-long slide. The same shape after a rally would be a shooting star. It has a real body, so it is not a gravestone doji. It still needs bullish confirmation before action.
questions.lesson_line: After a decline, a long upper shadow shows buyers tried. They still need the next candle to prove it.

wrong.Shooting star: Same shape, but a shooting star forms after an advance. This one came after a month-long slide.
wrong.Hammer: A hammer's long shadow is below the body. This one's is above.
wrong.Gravestone doji: A gravestone has open, low and close together, with no real body. This one closed at $22.50 against a $22.00 open, so it has a real body.

questions.simple: It is an inverted hammer: a long upper shadow and a small body near the low, after a long slide.

deeper.trap: The long upper shadow looks bearish, so it is easy to call it a shooting star. The trend decides the name. After a decline it is an inverted hammer. But it still shows a rally that failed by the close. So ChartSchool says bullish confirmation is required before action.

conflicts: Hammer vs hanging man: ChartSchool (Introduction to Candlesticks) and Investopedia (Hanging Man) say the two look identical and are named by the trend before them; the body can be black or white. Fidelity's webinar slides (citing Kirkpatrick and Dahlquist) say they are 'differentiated by the color of the body' and that hammers have white bodies and shooting stars black ones. The unit follows ChartSchool and Investopedia (q22, q27, w2) and asks no question about the color of a hammer, hanging man, inverted hammer or shooting star.

Harami colors: ChartSchool's Pattern Dictionary and Glossary H, and Investopedia's Candlestick page, say the second candle is the opposite color. ChartSchool's reversal-pattern pages (citing Nison's Beyond Candlesticks) and Fidelity's slides say any color combination counts. No question asks a harami's colors (q33, q35, q38 rest only on body inside body).

Engulfing and the shadows: ChartSchool (Dictionary, bullish and bearish pages), Investopedia's Bullish Engulfing page and Fidelity's slides judge engulfing on the bodies only. Investopedia's Bearish Engulfing page says the body is what matters 'not the changes in the wicks', but its next takeaway also says 'the high must be higher and the low must be lower'. q28, q29 and q30 key the body-only definition the sources share; q29 asks whether every engulfing is an outside day (False), which holds under the majority definition. Checker, 2026-11-09: Investopedia's Bullish Engulfing page has the same split: it says the body is judged 'without regard to the length of the tail shadows', then describes the second day opening 'lower than the previous low' and closing 'higher than the previous high'. ChartSchool states outright that engulfing 'does not require the entire range (high and low) to be engulfed', so q29 stands.

Doji strictness: Fidelity's slides say a doji's open and close are 'the same price'. ChartSchool ('virtually equal', 'Ideally, but not necessarily') and Investopedia ('the same or very close to it'; dragonfly page: 'slight discrepancies') allow a small difference. q10 keys the looser rule, held by two publishers.

Candle color: ChartSchool, Investopedia (Real Body), CME and Schwab say the color compares the close with the same candle's open; CME adds 'depending on the color settings of your software' and Fidelity says 'most commonly'. Investopedia's Candlestick page (Bottom Line) says the color shows the close against 'the previous period'. Checker, 2026-11-09: StockCharts' own SharpCharts FAQ (s36) says its default draws a candle black or red by the prior day's close and hollow or filled by the open, so a gap up that fades but closes above the prior close is a filled black candle there. The fill rule is the same everywhere: q53 now keys the fill only (it said 'Filled (red)'), q15 asks the convention ('most charting platforms') and names the StockCharts exception, and w1 says 'most charts'.

Dark cloud cover open: ChartSchool says the black candle opens above the previous close; Schwab says above the previous high; Investopedia lists a gap up. q31's story opens above both the prior close and the prior high, so it qualifies under all three; q32 asks only for the midpoint, which all three agree on.

Shooting star gap: ChartSchool reports Greg Morris wants a gap up while Nison shows one without, and concludes 'the essence of the reversal should not be lost without the gap'. q24's story does not mention a gap and its key does not rest on one.

Star: Investopedia's Star page describes the small body appearing 'above the prior candle's range' (the evening-star case). ChartSchool says a star gaps up or down. q42 keys 'gaps away', which covers both, and cites both pages.

Bar vs candle: Schwab says the candlestick chart 'offers traders more information' than a bar chart. CME ('a bar chart provides four pieces of data ... the open, high, low and close'; 'Candlestick charts take the same information as a bar chart') and Fidelity agree the two carry the same four prices; Schwab's 'more' reads as the visual body and color. q54 keys the same-four-prices fact.

Three white soldiers: ChartSchool says each close should be near the high of the day; Investopedia says each close exceeds the previous candle's high. q47 keys only what both say: three long white candles in a row, each opening inside the prior body.

Marubozu: ChartSchool's Introduction and Investopedia define the full marubozu, with no upper or lower shadow. ChartSchool's Pattern Dictionary also counts a candle with no shadow at only one end (the open or the close). q19, q20 and q21 use the full version, which both publishers share.

Sources left out on purpose: Thomas Bulkowski's ThePatternSite.com states the site 'shall not be used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems', and docs/study/TRAINING_CORPUS.md makes the whole Study module training material for UCT's own analysis system. To stay clear of that notice this unit cites no thepatternsite.com page; every key stands on ChartSchool, Investopedia, Schwab, Fidelity and CME. The owner may decide whether Bulkowski can be cited.
